{"id": "21:105/q14", "question": "How does this promise connect with its sūra and other Qur'anic promises?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding passage governs the promise: immediate afterlife context, earlier believers' reward, or broader prophet stories.", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q14/p1", "position": "It resumes the sūra's reminder and prophet stories and promises a good end for believers.", "reasons": "Biqai connects 21:10's reminder, David's story and the prophets' final outcome, linking 14:14, 7:128 and 23:11; he says a comparatively weak community receives what mighty David and Solomon had. Ibn Atiyya calls it reassurance after Israel's fulfilled promise. Islahi says the conclusion tells Prophet and companions to persist in the one prophetic message as judgment nears. Asad relates it to 3:139."}, {"id": "21:105/q14/p2", "position": "It follows the afterlife passage and foregrounds Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur notes the preceding Paradise passage and 39:73-74 and connects 21:44's shrinking earth; Razi and Alusi use immediate resurrection context; Islahi links the new earth to 21:104 and 14:48."}, {"id": "21:105/q14/p3", "position": "It completes the believers' reward account with a promise of worldly recompense.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the prior passage details afterlife reward and this one worldly recompense; he rejects the claim that adjacency to resurrection requires an afterlife-only interpretation. Ibn Ashur says it also comforts persecuted Meccan believers in this life, citing 16:97."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q15", "question": "Does after the Reminder imply the Zabur was created?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q15/p1", "position": "Yes, its coming after the Reminder demonstrates its createdness.", "reasons": "Jishumi makes this chronological theological inference."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q16", "question": "Why was this promise written for heavenly beings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q16/p1", "position": "For the angels' benefit.", "reasons": "Jishumi states this; Razi's account says future events were written in the Mother Book for angels before copying into prophetic books."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q17", "question": "What legal inference is drawn from this land promise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q17/p1", "position": "Jurists use it as strong proof that land differs from other cultivable property.", "reasons": "Zajjaj reports this juristic use without further elaboration."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q18", "question": "What reports connect the promise to end-time rule?", "turns_on": "Competing Mahdi reports and their chains; also whether the verse is applied to a wider end-time sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q18/p1", "position": "A righteous man or Mahdi from the Prophet's family will fill earth with justice.", "reasons": "Tabarsi quotes the one-day-prolonged report, a variant matching the Prophet's name, and Umm Salama's Fatima-descendant report; Abu Jaʿfar identifies his companions as heirs. Hakim judges explicit family Mahdi reports sounder. Kuranyolu describes end-time reform, order, peace, justice and fair distribution; Alusi allows universal rule with Mahdi and Jesus."}, {"id": "21:105/q18/p2", "position": "There is no Mahdi except Jesus.", "reasons": "The Anas report through Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Jundi says worsening affairs and miserliness precede an Hour coming only on wicked people. Hakim calls that transmitter unknown and notes conflicting chains, abandoned Aban ibn Abi Ayyash and a disconnected path."}, {"id": "21:105/q18/p3", "position": "A sequence of trials ends in righteous rule, resurrection and Paradise.", "reasons": "Elmalili describes about thirty false prophets, Dajjal's claim and death at the Messiah's descent, Gog and Magog's devastation and divine destruction, breaking cross and killing swine, universal Muhammadan law, then Beast, western sunrise, trumpet, resurrection, judgment and Paradise; hadith describes religion becoming strange before revival."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q19", "question": "What inward inheritance is read in the verse?", "turns_on": "Which inward domain or form of reward is meant by earth and inheritance.", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q19/p1", "position": "The heart's Psalter records the body's earth passing to illuminated faculties.", "reasons": "Qashani says discipline destroys vicious powers, letting righteous faculties inherit bodily life after the Preserved Tablet."}, {"id": "21:105/q19/p2", "position": "The soul's faculties inherit earth after annihilation in unity.", "reasons": "Qashani alternatively places writing in the Preserved Tablet after the Mother Book and names spirit, secret, heart, intellect, soul and faculties restored through uprightness."}, {"id": "21:105/q19/p3", "position": "The righteous inherit Paradise's ranks; lovers and knowers inherit witnessing divine majesty.", "reasons": "Ruzbihan's Araʾis as reported by Bursevi distinguishes servanthood's rewards from witnessing lordship; Bursevi also describes the soul's eternal return under the promise."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q20", "question": "Does this verse require an Imam for religious guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q20/p1", "position": "The Qur'an suffices for reflective guidance.", "reasons": "Jishumi uses the passage against the Imami claim that an Imam is required."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q21", "question": "What other Qur'an and earlier-scripture relations do these notes report?", "turns_on": "Different reported correspondences between Qur'anic divisions and earlier books, and whether earlier scriptures had suras.", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q21/p1", "position": "The Prophet received groups of Qur'anic suras in place of earlier books.", "reasons": "Wathila's versions align seven long suras with Torah, and vary between miʾun and mathani for Psalms or Gospel; all give Mufassal an extra distinction. Abu Qilaba swaps these groups; Ibn Masʿud gives Torah/long, Gospel/miʾun, Psalms/mathani. Baghawi's gharīb Wathila version adds Fatiha and Baqara's ending from beneath the Throne."}, {"id": "21:105/q21/p2", "position": "The Qur'an or an earlier book may receive a figurative name associated with another revelation.", "reasons": "Burhan lists Zabur among Qur'anic names with 6:115, 41:42, 3:193, 9:111, 2:97 and 80:13; Itqan reports a new Torah addressed to Muhammad and Moses' request for Ahmad's community, but says Torah and Gospel should no longer be applied as Qur'an names, comparing Torah as Furqan and Psalms as Qur'an in 2:53."}, {"id": "21:105/q21/p3", "position": "Qur'anic sura and verse names, divisions and virtues have distinct traditions.", "reasons": "Tabari attributes sura names to the Prophet and records Khalid's Mufassal as the Arabic, including a claim it has no prostration. Baghawi calls the Qur'an raises-and-lowers report sahih through Muslim and the ruined-house report sahih through Tirmidhi. Itqan records figurative sura grouping names, Ibn Masʿud's brocade for hawamim, Sakhawi's protective qawariʿ, and Verse of Might. Itqan says divisions show independent inimitability and aid teaching; Zarkashi says earlier books lacked suras, Zamakhshari says they had them, which Itqan prefers; Qatada gives Psalms 150 praise suras without law. Itqan also reports the refuge suras' unique status and their recitation protections."}, {"id": "21:105/q21/p4", "position": "Other vocabulary surveys supply comparisons but no alternative reading of this verse.", "reasons": "Damghani's thirteen uses of earth include Mecca, Egypt, Islamic lands, grave, wilderness, resurrection land, heart and mosque courtyard; Itqan transmits Ibn Abbas's general glosses of tasbih, sultan, din, rayb, qunut, alim, qatl and rijz. Elmalili lists the Qur'an's names al-Huda and al-Nur with 2:185, 3:4 and 7:157."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q22", "question": "How is the possessive yāʾ in My servants read?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive yāʾ is still or opened before al-salihun.", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q22/p1", "position": "Hamza gives the possessive yāʾ sukūn.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid, Qurtubi, Nasafi and Nashr identify Hamza; Nashr notes his consistent treatment of fourteen disputed yāʾs before hamzat wasl and article; Qiraat-ER says the sound changes without changing sense."}, {"id": "21:105/q22/p2", "position": "The other readers open this yāʾ with fatḥa.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid and Nasafi contrast the others with Hamza; Nashr says the readers agree on fatḥa for a separate remaining set of eighteen yāʾs."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q23", "question": "Can a conquest date be inferred from this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q23/p1", "position": "A famous decoding linked it to Sultan Selim's conquest of Egypt.", "reasons": "Alusi reports the Ibn Kamal story but says its success was coincidence and gives it no evidential weight."}]}
{"id": "21:105/q24", "question": "What happened when the Prophet attended battle?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:105/q24/p1", "position": "He prayed for God to judge with truth.", "reasons": "Qatada transmits this report in Abd al-Razzaq."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q01", "question": "What does 'that' refer to and how does it introduce this statement?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative resumes the preceding rites, supplies an elliptical predication or command, or marks a discourse transition.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q01/p1", "position": "It sums up the prescribed pilgrimage acts just mentioned.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies removing dishevelment, fulfilling vows, and circumambulating the Ancient House; Tabataba'i extends the summary back to Abraham's rites, prayer, sacrifice and pure worship. Islahi reads a close to Abraham's directions and an address to negligent heirs."}, {"id": "22:30/q01/p2", "position": "It is a discourse transition, 'the matter is thus,' with an omitted subject or predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq make it nominative; Zamakhshari compares an author's transi

tion, and Samin prefers an omitted subject. Ibn Ashur instead makes 'that' a fronted subject whose predicate is omitted. Zuhayr's line and 38:55 exemplify the usage; the remote demonstrative dignifies the prior matter."}, {"id": "22:30/q01/p3", "position": "It means 'your prescribed obligation is that.'", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya supplies 'your obligation' or 'the obligation' as the omitted element; Qurtubi also allows this nominative construction."}, {"id": "22:30/q01/p4", "position": "It is an accusative object of an implied command to perform or obey what preceded.", "reasons": "Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Alusi record the omitted command as 'carry out,' 'comply with,' or 'follow.'"}, {"id": "22:30/q01/p5", "position": "It is a nominative topic with an omitted predicate referring back to the previous matter.", "reasons": "Samin and Abu Hayyan report this alternative; Nasafi permits 'let them do that' alongside 'the matter is that.'"}, {"id": "22:30/q01/p6", "position": "It sums up pilgrimage's great worldly and otherworldly benefits.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i takes the pointing word to refer to the great pilgrimage and its benefits."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q02", "question": "What are God's inviolable things and what does honoring them require?", "turns_on": "Whether the term covers all divine limits, pilgrimage duties or prohibitions, a list of sacred places and states, or inward disciplines.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q02/p1", "position": "They include all divine obligations, commands, prohibitions, and sacred things; honoring them means obeying and preserving them.", "reasons": "Al-Layth defines hurma as what may not be violated, and al-Zajjaj as what must be upheld. Wahidi prefers Ibn Abbas's obligations and Sunna as most comprehensive; Abu Hayyan prefers the general sense. Qurtubi includes recommended acts; Razi reports theologians excluding supererogatory acts. Zajjaj includes Hajj and Umra. Elmalili includes sacred places. Tabari and Durr transmit Mujahid's combined list; Ibn Jawzi repeats the lexical rule that violation is unlawful."}, {"id": "22:30/q02/p2", "position": "They are specifically the rites of Hajj and Umra, honored by performing them.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba names pebble casting and standing at Jamʿ or Muzdalifa. Surrounding 22:29 motivates the narrower sense for Baghawi, Tabarsi and Qurtubi. Al-Kalbi emphasizes performing prescribed rites; Ibn Ashur adds sacrificial animals, garlands and the sacred site and prefers this breadth over a fixed list."}, {"id": "22:30/q02/p3", "position": "They are God's forbidden acts or sins, especially prohibitions during ihram; honoring means refraining.", "reasons": "Ata and Ikrima gloss sanctities as sins. Ibn Abbas specifies intercourse, sin, quarrels and hunting in consecration. Tabari, Ibn Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and Tabataba'i stress not crossing divine limits."}, {"id": "22:30/q02/p4", "position": "They are named sacred sites, times and states: the House, Mosque, territory, month, and pilgrim in consecration.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's lists vary: some include Sacred Station or Landmark and some omit month or ihram. Zayd ibn Aslam's five include the Kaaba, Mosque, land, month, and person or site in consecration. Wahidi links the list to 2:194, as does Tabarsi."}, {"id": "22:30/q02/p5", "position": "Inwardly, sanctities include spiritual practice and reverence preserving faith.", "reasons": "Qushayri stresses jealous care for faith and warns that neglect of service brings punishment, while neglected reverence risks separation and disturbed oneness. Bursevi says obedience reaches Paradise but reverence brings nearness to God. Qashani includes self-offering, purification, virtue, disclosures and stations."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q03", "question": "What does 'it is better for him with his Lord' mean and what does 'it' resume?", "turns_on": "Whether khayr is comparative or absolute good; all connect the gain to reverence.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q03/p1", "position": "Honoring the sanctities earns good or reward with God in the afterlife.", "reasons": "The pronoun resumes the verbal noun of 'honor,' as Wahidi, Samin and Ibn Ashur explain; Nahhas parses subject and predicate. Ibn Abbas calls the benefit increased obedience and fear. Razi and Ibn al-Shaykh read 'with his Lord' as stored reward. Alusi says the possessive 'his Lord' honors the person."}, {"id": "22:30/q03/p2", "position": "'Better' is comparative: reverence benefits one more than neglect or taking sanctities lightly.", "reasons": "Al-Asamm explicitly contrasts veneration with treating sanctities lightly; Samin accepts the apparent comparative sense with interpretive qualification."}, {"id": "22:30/q03/p3", "position": "'Good' is a promise of good, without an implied comparison.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this alternative; Abu Hayyan says no comparator need be supplied, and Alusi transmits that observation."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q04", "question": "What livestock does God make lawful and under what basic rule?", "turns_on": "Whether livestock is read as actual sacrificial and edible animals or inwardly as sound souls.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q04/p1", "position": "Camels, cattle, sheep and goats—the eight male and female pairs—may be slaughtered and eaten; pagan dedicated or taboo categories remain lawful.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Kathir name bahira, saiba, wasila, hami, and idol-dedicated beasts. Bursevi excludes horses, mules and donkeys. Alusi notes lawful action is slaughter or eating rather than the animal itself. Asad says what revelation does not explicitly prohibit is lawful. Ibn Jawzi points to the livestock discussion at 5:1."}, {"id": "22:30/q04/p2", "position": "Inwardly, lawful cattle are sound souls whose moral qualities and actions may be used on the path.", "reasons": "Qashani says the wayfarer uses the soul's rights rather than personal interest."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q05", "question": "What does 'except what is recited to you' exclude?", "turns_on": "Whether the recited exception names forbidden food categories, game in consecration, or an inward analogue.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q05/p1", "position": "It excludes the scripturally forbidden foods, especially carrion, blood, pork, offerings to other than God and animals dying by strangling, blows, falls, goring or predators.", "reasons": "Most cite 5:3 or 5:1; Ibn Ashur cites prior Meccan prohibitions in 6:145 and al-Nahl, whereas Tabataba'i cites al-An'am, al-Nahl and al-Baqara. Qatada singles out carrion and animals over which God's name was not pronounced. Tabataba'i says pilgrimage context especially targets pagan offerings at the Kaaba, Safa, Marwa and Mina. This exception never reinstates pagan bahira or saiba bans."}, {"id": "22:30/q05/p2", "position": "It excludes hunting or game during ihram.", "reasons": "Yahya links the restriction to 5:1. Thalabi, Mawardi, Ibn Jawzi and Qurtubi transmit the alternative; Razi says the clause prevents confusing livestock with game."}, {"id": "22:30/q05/p3", "position": "Inwardly, the exceptions are vices disguised as virtues.", "reasons": "Qashani calls acts of the soul in an improper mode forbidden to wayfarers."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q06", "question": "How is the exception grammatically attached?", "turns_on": "Whether prohibited cases remain members of the livestock class or the recited list extends beyond it.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q06/p1", "position": "The exception is accusative and connected: some livestock become forbidden by an incidental cause.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Zajjaj call mā accusative. Samin and Bursevi give death as a contingent cause; Alusi says this is the majority analysis and cites carrion and offerings to another."}, {"id": "22:30/q06/p2", "position": "The exception is disconnected because livestock are not intrinsically forbidden or some listed foods are not livestock.", "reasons": "Samin refers to the argument at 5:1; Alusi reports that the list of 5:3 includes non-livestock items."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q07", "question": "Why say 'is recited' in the present tense?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperfect evokes a past recitation, recurrence, or an already current recitation rather than a future reference.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q07/p1", "position": "The present evokes an already recited prohibition with emphasis, not necessarily future revelation.", "reasons": "Alusi says the prohibition verse had already been recited."}, {"id": "22:30/q07/p2", "position": "The present marks continuing and repeated recitation.", "reasons": "Alusi reports the contextual reading; Ibn Ashur covers earlier recitation continuing into the present and later revelation such as 5:103."}, {"id": "22:30/q07/p3", "position": "It means prohibitions already being recited, with no need to anticipate the later Ma'idah verse.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i prefers this because food bans appear in al-An'am, al-Nahl and al-Baqara; Ibn Ashur likewise points to earlier Meccan verses."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q08", "question": "Why is livestock permission inserted among the pilgrimage commands?", "turns_on": "Whether its chief link is correcting animal law in Hajj or preparing the return to prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q08/p1", "position": "It corrects pagan animal taboos and clarifies that ihram does not forbid livestock as it forbids game.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites 6:139 and 5:103; Razi, Bursevi and Alusi describe possible confusion in consecration. Qurtubi connects the rule to animals sacrificed at Hajj; Ibn Ashur to 6:145. Samarra'i notes 22:28 and 22:34 specify bahimat al-an'am after general remembrance, while this verse names livestock directly."}, {"id": "22:30/q08/p2", "position": "It prepares the later commands by distinguishing God's limits from idols and false claims about animals.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i prefers the sanctities sentence as preparation; Alusi says the exception eases transition to the idol ban. {"id": "22:30/q09", "question": "What does 'avoid' require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q09/p1", "position": "Keep well away, leave aside, and do not approach the prohibited thing.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives the lexical sense of distance; Ibn Jawzi says to leave the abomination; Razi and Bursevi extend avoidance to every form of false speech."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q10", "question": "What does rijs mean here, and why are idols so called?", "turns_on": "Whether impurity belongs to idols as moral or legal filth, a disparaging figure, blood on the objects, or related gambling.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q10/p1", "position": "It means foulness or impurity; idols are figuratively or legally filthy because their worship is sinful, causes punishment, or deserves revulsion.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba contrasts rijs, stench or filth, with rijz, torment, citing 9:125, 10:100, 7:134 and 8:11. Wahidi says an idol is not physical dirt; Razi rejects physical impurity. Kashshaf compares wine, gambling and divining arrows at 5:90. Qurtubi reports impurity as legal status removed by faith; Bursevi distinguishes natural, rational and legal impurity."}, {"id": "22:30/q10/p2", "position": "Idols are called rijs to disparage and belittle them.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this explanation to Al-Asamm's blood account; Baydawi says comparison to repulsive filth intensifies the ban."}, {"id": "22:30/q10/p3", "position": "Rijs is sacrificial blood smeared on idols.", "reasons": "A reported account says polytheists covered idols in blood. Al-Asamm offers this rationale; Razi rejects it as far-fetched."}, {"id": "22:30/q10/p4", "position": "Imami reports extend the prohibited filth to chess, backgammon and other gambling.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Tabataba'i transmit these reports."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q11", "question": "What does awthan mean, and how is the word explained?", "turns_on": "Whether the term denotes erected worship objects only or also whatever the self treats as an object of worship.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q11/p1", "position": "Awthan are erected objects worshipped as idols, made of stone, wood or metal; a cross can be called a wathan.", "reasons": "Shammar lists wood, stone, gold, silver and copper. Al-A'sha calls the Christian cross a wathan; reports from Adi ibn Hatim say the Prophet called his gold cross an idol. Bursevi transmits a distinction between a human-shaped sanam and a less fashioned wathan, while Mufradat says worshipped stones."}, {"id": "22:30/q11/p2", "position": "Wathan derives from standing fixed in place.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan cite the related word wathin; Ru'ba's line illustrates steadfastness in an old bond or covenant."}, {"id": "22:30/q11/p3", "position": "In a wider reading, idols include false beliefs, values, practices and enslaving desires.", "reasons": "Asad extends concrete idols to worshipped values; Qushayri says one's followed desire and self become one's idol; Qashani cites 45:23."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q12", "question": "What does 'the filth of idols' command one to avoid?", "turns_on": "Whether the object of avoidance is idols as such, their worship or other attached idolatrous practices.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q12/p1", "position": "It forbids worshipping idols and obeying Satan in that worship.", "reasons": "Tabari says all idols are rijs and rejects the claim that the phrase singles out only some; Ibn Abbas emphasizes not obeying Satan. Wahidi reports the worship brings curse, punishment or sin. The wording extends avoidance to the object to intensify the ban, as Tabataba'i notes."}, {"id": "22:30/q12/p2", "position": "It commands avoiding the idols themselves as impure objects.", "reasons": "Zajjaj's and Tabarsi's explanatory reading identifies the rijs as the idol; Ibn Ashur says it clarifies what lies outside God's sanctities. Al-Kur'an Yolu attributes this view to Ibn Ashur."}, {"id": "22:30/q12/p3", "position": "It includes cleansing the House and keeping away from tangible as well as spiritual filth.", "reasons": "Elmalili connects slaughter in God's name with removal of idols and distinguishes carrion's tangible filth from idolatry's spiritual filth."}, {"id": "22:30/q12/p4", "position": "It may cover offerings dedicated to other than God as an expression of ingratitude.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a causal reading tied to livestock permission and the later 'not associating'; he objects that lawful status itself does not prove monotheism."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q13", "question": "What is the force of min in 'the filth of idols'?", "turns_on": "Whether min identifies the idol as the kind of rijs, a defiling aspect of it, its source, or adds no semantic relation.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q13/p1", "position": "It explains or specifies the kind: the filth is idols.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Abu Ishaq, grammarians, and most exegetes support this; Kashshaf compares specifying dirhams, Mubarrad cites 48:29 and Sibawayh. Razi says it cannot imply only some idols are filth. Burhan tests substitution with alladhi. Tabataba'i prefers this and calls alternatives strained."}, {"id": "22:30/q13/p2", "position": "It is partitive: the filth arising from idols is the forbidden act of worshipping them.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash calls this rare but good, and Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj allow the idols' use for building while prohibiting worship. Ibn Abi al-Rabi prefers it and cites 39:17. Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi object that it corrupts the sense; Alusi rejects their objection but finds the reading strained."}, {"id": "22:30/q13/p3", "position": "It marks the origin or starting point of filth in idol worship.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says idol worship gathers all corruption; later Maghribi grammarians say impurity is broader than idols. Alusi considers this reading strained."}, {"id": "22:30/q13/p4", "position": "It is an extra particle.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports the analysis without further support."}, {"id": "22:30/q13/p5", "position": "The explanatory and source senses can be combined here.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa proposed the blend; Samin rejects the conflation."}]}
{"id": "22:30/q14", "question": "What is meant by 'false speech'?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression remains a general ban on falsehood or is focused on shirk, a pilgrimage formula, false testimony, fabricated food law, or inward and other speech.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q14/p1", "position": "It is all lies and falsehood, including slander and fabricated speech against God.", "reasons": "Mujahid glosses lying. Zajjaj accepts lying, shirk and false testimony together. Tabari names claims that idols mediate at 39:3 and that angels are daughters. Biqa'i includes falsehood deviating from proof. Alusi and Razi treat specific applications as included without narrowing the general ban; Alusi prefers this breadth."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p2", "position": "It is associating partners with God or idolatrous speech.", "reasons": "Yahya says lying about God is shirk; Ibn Abbas calls it fabrication and denial. Claims that idols deserve worship or that angels are God's daughters are examples. Asad links this wider false worship to untrue speech."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p3", "position": "It especially means the polytheists' pilgrimage talbiya naming a partner God supposedly owns.", "reasons": "Muhammad b. Ali names Quraysh, Khuza'a, Kinana and Amir b. Sa'sa'a, referring to worshipped angels. Later reports quote the formula's claimed partner and possessions; Jishumi gives it as an occasion of revelation."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p4", "position": "It means false testimony.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud and Wa'il are cited for the interpretation; prophetic reports compare false testimony with shirk. Qurtubi, Baydawi, and Alusi transmit it; Alusi says the report does not prove exclusivity."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p5", "position": "It includes invented dietary rulings that call lawful animals forbidden or forbidden meat lawful.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites 6:139 and 5:103; Abu Ishaq cites bahira and saiba. Baydawi, Ibn Ashur and Elmalili tie this to pagan attribution of animal taboos to God."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p6", "position": "It means hypocrisy or speech whose tongue belies the heart.", "reasons": "Mawardi gives outward Islam with inward falsehood; Qushayri and Bursevi include broken inner covenants. Qashani gives embellished speculative sciences and disputatious doubts."}, {"id": "22:30/q14/p7", "position": "It includes singing and frivolous or distracting speech.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Tabataba'i transmit Imami reports."}]}

{"id": "22:30/q19", "question": "Why do the idol and false-speech commands follow the sanctities and livestock clauses?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence is grounded in sanctities and the broadening of falsehood, pagan animal rules, or gratitude for livestock.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q19/p1", "position": "Monotheism and truth are foremost sanctities; the verse moves from idol worship, the chief falsehood, to all false speech.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Alusi and others say shirk falsely ascribes divine worth to idols. {"id": "22:30/q20", "question": "How do the particles, pronouns, and repeated commands sharpen the wording?", "turns_on": "Which small form is being explained: consequence, emphasis, anaphora, or possessive honor.", "positions": [{"id": "22:30/q20/p1", "position": "The fa makes idol avoidance follow the duty to honor God's sanctities.", "reasons": "Alusi identifies the preceding implication; Tabataba'i likewise reads a consequence."}, {"id": "22:30/q20/p2", "position": "The repeated imperative separately emphasizes avoiding false speech.", "reasons": "Alusi says direct coordination would be weaker; Burhan notes the shift from past-tense permission to imperative, as in 7:29."}, {"id": "22:30/q20/p3", "position": "The pronoun 'it' resumes the act of honoring expressed by the verb.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Samin explain the verbal noun implicit in yu'azzim; Ibn Ashur concurs and Samin compares 5:8."}, {"id": "22:30/q20/p4", "position": "The possessive 'his Lord' honors the reverent person and explains the promised reward.", "reasons": "Alusi states this rhetorical function."}]}

{"id": "23:1/q10", "question": "What conditions make the believers successful?", "turns_on": "The sources give both the listed practices and an account of the active faith that generates them.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q10/p1", "position": "Faith must bear the worship and ethical traits listed in the opening passage.", "reasons": "Tabari names belief in God and Messenger, acceptance of revelation and these deeds.
